title: First Council of Nicaea
blurb: The first ecumenical council, summoned by Constantine, defined the Son as homoousios — of the same essence as the Father — against Arius. The Nicene Creed dates from this gathering.

title: First Council of Constantinople
blurb: Reaffirmed Nicaea, condemned Macedonianism (denial of the Spirit's divinity), and gave the creed its final shape — the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed Christians still recite.

title: Council of Ephesus
blurb: Condemned Nestorius for separating the divine and human in Christ, and affirmed Mary as Theotokos — God-bearer. Cyril of Alexandria carried the day.

title: Council of Chalcedon
blurb: Defined Christ as one person in two natures — divine and human, unconfused, unchanged, undivided, unseparated. Pope Leo's Tome was read aloud and accepted.

title: Second Council of Constantinople
blurb: Condemned the Three Chapters and posthumously censured Origen, attempting to reconcile the Eastern miaphysites without conceding Chalcedon.

title: Third Council of Constantinople
blurb: Condemned Monothelitism and affirmed two wills in Christ, divine and human — vindicating Maximus the Confessor, who had died for the doctrine eighteen years earlier.

title: Second Council of Nicaea
blurb: Restored the veneration of icons after the first iconoclast crisis, distinguishing veneration (proskynesis) from worship (latreia). The last council both East and West accept as ecumenical.

title: Council of Carthage
blurb: Confirmed the canon of Scripture for the Latin West — the same 73-book canon Augustine defended and Jerome reluctantly translated.

title: Second Council of Orange
blurb: Settled the Semi-Pelagian controversy, affirming Augustine's doctrine of grace: faith itself is a gift, not a human initiative God then assists.

title: Arius condemned at Nicaea
blurb: The council's anathemas drew the line: anyone teaching that the Son was created, or that there was when he was not, is outside the Church.

title: Nestorius condemned at Ephesus
blurb: Nestorius's refusal to call Mary Theotokos cost him his see. Cyril's twelve anathemas became the test of orthodoxy in the East.

title: Pelagius condemned at Carthage
blurb: The African council, with Augustine's pen behind it, ruled that grace is necessary not only for choosing good but for knowing it — the formal end of Pelagian optimism.

title: Eutyches condemned at Chalcedon
blurb: His claim that Christ's humanity was absorbed into his divinity — one nature after the union — was rejected as a denial of true incarnation.

title: Origen condemned at Constantinople II
blurb: Three centuries after his death, Origen's speculations on pre-existent souls and universal restoration were anathematized — a closing of the door his admirers had kept ajar.

title: Acacian Schism begins
blurb: Pope Felix III excommunicated Acacius of Constantinople over the Henotikon. The first formal break between Rome and Constantinople; healed in 519, but the pattern was set.

title: Three Chapters controversy
blurb: Justinian's posthumous condemnation of three Antiochene theologians split the West — North Africa and Aquileia broke communion with Rome over the imperial overreach.

title: Iconoclasm imposed in the East
blurb: Emperor Leo III ordered the destruction of icons. The West refused; John of Damascus, safe under Muslim rule, wrote three orations defending images.

title: Donatist schism opens in Africa
blurb: Donatus refused communion with bishops who had handed over scriptures during persecution. Augustine spent decades arguing them down, with mixed results.

title: Novatian schism in Rome
blurb: Novatian rejected Cornelius's leniency toward Christians who had lapsed under Decius. The first major split over discipline rather than doctrine.

title: Death of John of Damascus — patristic age closes
blurb: The last of the Greek Fathers dies at Mar Saba. With him, the patristic age proper ends; what comes next is medieval theology, working from his synthesis.

title: Council of Jerusalem
blurb: Peter, Paul, and James settled the question of Gentile circumcision. The first conciliar decision in Christian history; recorded in Acts 15.

title: Edict of Milan
blurb: Constantine and Licinius granted toleration to Christians across the empire. The persecution era ended; the institutional church began.

title: Sack of Rome by Alaric
blurb: Pagans blamed Christianity for the city's fall. Augustine's reply, the City of God, recast history itself: two cities, two loves, only one eternal.

title: Third Council of Toledo
blurb: Visigothic Spain converted from Arianism to Catholic Christianity. The filioque — the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son — first appears in conciliar form here.

title: Synod of Whitby
blurb: Northumbria chose Roman over Celtic Christianity — the dating of Easter, the shape of the tonsure, the line of authority. Bede tells the story with characteristic care.
